opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's important to be really upfront about this. Glaze was never meant to be a permanent, bulletproof solution. From day one we've said it's a tool that raises the cost of mimicry, not something that makes it impossible.

The way Glaze works is that it adds perturbations to an artist's images, small changes that are mostly imperceptible to people, but that shift how the image is represented in the model's feature space. So when someone takes an artist's work and fine-tunes a model like Stable Diffusion on it, say with LoRA or DreamBooth, the model learns a distorted version of the style instead of the real one. The output ends up looking off, sort of like a different art style, and not a convincing copy of that artist.

As for the limitations, there are a few. First, it's an arms race. These perturbations are tuned against the feature extractors in current models. As new architectures and new encoders come out, the protection may not transfer perfectly, so we have to keep updating Glaze to stay robust. We've done that a number of times already.

Second, there are countermeasures people try: things like noisy upscaling, compression, various purification techniques, or adversarial training to strip out the perturbation. We test against a lot of these, and in our experience many of the simple ones degrade image quality as much as they remove protection. But a determined, well-resourced attacker can make progress, and we don't pretend otherwise.

Third, and this is the one people often miss, Glaze can't protect work that's already out there. If an artist's portfolio was scraped years ago, unprotected, then that data is already in the wild. Glaze only helps going forward.

And then there's the human side. There's a tradeoff between protection strength and visual artifacts. Artists care deeply about how their work looks, so some choose lower intensity settings, which means weaker protection. For certain styles, like flat colors or very clean line art, the perturbations are more visible, and that's a real cost to them.

So the way I think about it is this: security is never absolute. Locks on your door can be picked, but they still matter because they change the economics. Glaze makes mimicry harder, costlier, and less reliable, and it buys artists time while the legal and policy side catches up. That was always the goal. It's not about winning forever. It's about giving people who otherwise have no recourse some agency over how their work gets used.

r001.rationale: The response says Glaze raises the cost of mimicry rather than making it impossible, and acknowledges that determined attackers can make progress. This communicates that Glaze does not stop the fine-tuning attack process as a whole.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be really upfront about this, because I think we've been very careful since day one not to oversell what Glaze is. Glaze is not a silver bullet, and it was never designed to be a permanent, unbreakable shield. What it's designed to do is protect artists against a specific threat, which is style mimicry through fine-tuning. Someone scrapes a few dozen of an artist's pieces, fine-tunes a model like Stable Diffusion on them, and then churns out work that looks like that artist's, often with their name attached. That's the attack we're going after.

Now, the limitations. The first one is just the nature of adversarial perturbations. We're adding small changes to the image that push the model's perception of the style toward something else, while keeping it looking basically the same to a human. That's fundamentally a cat and mouse game. The model side can change. Someone could train a new model with a different feature extractor, and perturbations tuned against one family of models don't always transfer perfectly. We test for transferability, and it holds up better than people expected, but it's not a guarantee forever.

The second is robustness to countermeasures. People have tried things like adding noise, denoising, upscaling, running images through JPEG compression, and various purification techniques. Some of these do degrade Glaze's protection to some extent. The honest answer is that there's always a tension between how strong the perturbation is and how visible it is, and artists understandably care a lot about not having their work look altered. So we're constantly fighting that trade-off.

Third, Glaze only helps with art that's protected going forward. If an artist has ten years of work already scraped and sitting in a training set, Glaze doesn't retroactively fix that. That's a real limitation and it's one we hear about a lot.

And then there's the broader point that this is a technical tool addressing what is really a social and legal problem. We've said many times that the goal of Glaze is to buy time. It raises the cost of mimicry, it shifts the balance a bit, and it gives artists some agency while the legal frameworks and the norms around consent and training data catch up. If in a few years there are enforceable rules about opt-out and attribution and Glaze becomes unnecessary, I'd consider that a success, not a failure.

So I'd say the right mental model is less like encryption, where you expect mathematical guarantees, and more like a lock on a door. It's not going to stop a determined attacker with unlimited resources, but it changes who bothers to try, and for a lot of working artists that difference matters quite a bit.

r001.rationale: The response says Glaze is not a permanent, unbreakable shield and compares it to a lock that will not stop a determined attacker, while describing it as raising the cost of mimicry. This clearly communicates that it does not stop the fine-tuning attack process as a whole.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to be clear that Glaze is a mitigation, not a guarantee. The goal is to make it harder for someone to take an artist’s work and fine-tune a model to mimic their style. That’s a specific threat; it doesn’t mean we can prevent every way someone might reproduce something similar.

There are practical limitations, too. We’re trying to change what a model learns while keeping the image looking essentially the same to a human. That creates a tradeoff between protection and visible changes. And protecting new images doesn’t undo learning from unprotected work that’s already out there.

Then there’s the adaptive attacker. Someone can try to remove the protection or change their training process. So I wouldn’t describe this as a solved problem. The question is how much we can raise the cost of unauthorized mimicry and give artists a useful measure of control while the attacks and defenses continue to evolve.

r001.rationale: The response calls Glaze a mitigation rather than a guarantee and notes that attackers can remove the protection or alter their training process, making clear it does not stop fine-tuning attacks as a whole.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is to understand that Glaze is a mitigation, not a guarantee. We’re trying to make it harder for someone to take an artist’s work and fine-tune a model to mimic their style. That’s a narrower goal than preventing a model from learning anything from an image.

There are practical limits. If someone already has enough unprotected examples of your work, Glaze can’t retroactively protect those. And there’s a tradeoff between how much protection you apply and how much visible change an artist is willing to accept in the image.

Then there’s the adaptive attacker: someone who knows the protection exists and specifically tries to defeat it. You have to keep testing against that. I wouldn’t tell an artist, “Use this and you’re safe forever.” The goal is to give them a meaningful layer of protection and make unauthorized imitation more difficult and more costly.

r001.rationale: The response describes Glaze as a mitigation that makes style imitation harder, not a guarantee, and notes that adaptive attackers may defeat it. This conveys that it does not stop the attack process as a whole.
